Knowledge center/How I work

Measurement

How neon1 defines success with you, measures it, and reports what the numbers can and can't show.

Type
Standard
Edition
1.0
First written
November 1, 2026
Updated
November 9, 2026
Download PDF

Measurement shows whether the work was worth it. It starts during discovery with a baseline, gets checked at handover, and gets reviewed after real use. I keep the list short, define every number exactly, and say plainly what a small sample can't prove.

Terms

TermMeaning
MeasurementOne observation, such as 18 completed requests
MetricA defined way to measure, such as completed requests divided by valid attempts
KPIA metric chosen because it matters to an ongoing goal. "Key" should keep the list short
BaselineWhere things stood before, under stated conditions
TargetThe result we're aiming for
GuardrailSomething that must not get worse while we improve the main result
OKRAn objective plus a few measurable key results by a date

Publishing a page is a task. People understanding it and acting on it is an outcome. I try to measure outcomes.

Every measure gets a definition

Each measure we agree on gets a metric record: what decision it supports, exactly what counts, the formula, the source, the baseline, the target, and the review date. A zero in the denominator means "no data," not zero percent and not perfect. Missing data stays visible as unknown.

Measures I reach for most

MeasureDefinitionWatch out for
Task completionFinished tasks ÷ valid attemptsA page loading isn't a completed booking
First time rightCases needing no correction ÷ completed casesSay how long corrections are watched for
Hands-on timeTime a person actively works a caseKeep it apart from waiting, and include new review time
End-to-end timeFinish time minus valid request timeInclude queues and handoffs
Net time savedOld effort minus new effort minus new review and upkeepCompare like with like, and don't count saved time twice
Error rateCases with a defined error ÷ cases checkedState severity and how you checked
AdoptionPeople or cases using the new way ÷ those eligibleForced use isn't satisfaction
Independent successPeople finishing without help ÷ people tryingWith a few people, it's qualitative evidence
Benefit realizedObserved benefit ÷ estimated benefit, same periodKeep time, money, and quality apart unless the conversion is written down

Satisfaction scores such as CSAT and NPS have their place. With a handful of clients, a direct conversation about what worked and what's still hard usually tells us more.

Small samples

  • Counts appear next to percentages. Four out of five is 80%, and one more case changes it a lot.
  • Failed and abandoned cases stay in the data.
  • A survey only happy customers answer overstates satisfaction.
  • Zero failures in 20 representative trials still allows a failure rate near 14% at 95% confidence. A small pilot finds problems. It can't prove near-perfection. (The math follows NIST's handbook.)
  • Seasons, staff changes, and training also move numbers, so before-and-after reports name them. I don't claim cause and effect without a design that could show it.

What a report from me looks like

One page when possible: the result you wanted, the period and sample size, the baseline, what we see now, cost and effort, failures and exceptions, what the numbers can't establish, and the next decision. Quotes appear only with permission. The question it answers is whether the change is worth keeping.

Software and website measures

For software I track how often changes ship, how long they take, how often they fail, and how fast service comes back. For websites I check Core Web Vitals and test accessibility against WCAG 2.2 AA on the real pages. An automated accessibility score is a starting point, not a certificate.
